grammar.title: 3A: Choosing between comparatives and superlatives
grammar.explanation:
Use **comparative adjective + than** when you compare two people, places, or things. Think of comparing a frugal budget with a lavish one.

Spelling follows simple rules: **-er for short adjectives**, **more for long ones**. Double the final consonant after a short vowel (big → bigger); change y to i (thrifty → thriftier).

Three adjectives are irregular: **good → better, bad → worse, far → further / farther**. Use further for abstract distance and figurative ideas.

Use **(not) as + adjective + as** to say things are equal, or not equal. It compares a thrifty choice with an exorbitant one without ranking them.

Comparative **adverbs** compare actions: **-er for short adverbs** (drive faster), **more for -ly adverbs** (spend more carefully). Haggle more patiently and you will pay less.

Use **the + superlative** to pick one item out of a whole group. The most affluent customer is not always the smartest shopper.

Form superlatives like comparatives: **-est for short adjectives**, **most / least for long ones**. That boutique charges the highest markup on the street.

After a superlative, use **in, not of**, for places and groups. Say the cheapest hotel in the city, never of the city.

Superlatives often pair with the **present perfect + ever**. It frames a windfall as a once-in-a-lifetime event.

Use **the same as** to say two things are identical. A buyer hoping to recoup a loss treats every price tag the same as the next.

At C1 level, sharpen comparatives with **much, far, a lot, slightly, or a little**. A windfall saved is far better than a windfall squandered.

You can also soften a comparison with **less + adjective**. A less lavish wedding can be more memorable than an exorbitant one.
examples: A frugal lifestyle is *healthier* than a lavish one. (comparative + than)
A thrifty shopper often ends up *better* off than an affluent overspender. (irregular: good → better)
She learned to haggle *more patiently* than her brother. (comparative adverb)
That shop charges the *highest* markup in the whole district. (superlative + in, not of)
It was the most exorbitant meal we have *ever* tasted. (superlative + present perfect + ever)
His new budget is not *as lavish as* his old one. ((not) as + adjective + as)
A windfall saved is *far better* than a windfall squandered. (intensifier + comparative)
She is *as thrifty as* her grandmother was. (as + adjective + as)
They chose a *less lavish* wedding and saved a fortune. (less + adjective)
He treats every price tag *the same as* the next when he tries to recoup a loss. (the same as)

practice.q: Which is correct: 'This phone is expensiver than mine' or 'This phone is more expensive than mine'?
practice.a: The second one. Long adjectives use more, not -er: more expensive than.

practice.q: Complete the sentence: 'It was the ___ (bad) meal I've ever had.'
practice.a: 'the worst' — the superlative of bad, often paired with the present perfect + ever.

practice.q: Is 'the cheapest hotel of the city' correct?
practice.a: No. After a superlative use in, not of: the cheapest hotel in the city.
